headline: Google surges nearly 7% last night on strong earnings while the ASX closed up 0.47% — but Iran tensions and crashing oil prices are the big stories shaping global markets.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: GOOG had a massive night last session, jumping 6.88% to $356.65 USD. The surge was driven by a blowout Q4 earnings report — revenue growth and AI-driven cloud demand came in well above expectations, reassuring investors that Google is holding its own in the AI race against Microsoft.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft jumped 3.02% to $464.72 USD last session after its own strong Q4 earnings — cloud revenue soared and Azure (its cloud computing business) posted impressive growth. The market rewarded both Google and Microsoft in the same session, a rare double win for big tech.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two slipped 1.82% to $242.92 USD last session. No major negative news — the dip likely reflects some profit-taking after recent gains. GTA 6 gameplay footage is reportedly dropping this month, which remains a big catalyst on the horizon.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS fell 1.69% today to $4.08, continuing its tough run. Lithium prices remain subdued globally and there's no near-term catalyst to push the price higher. The stock is still well off its highs and remains a long-term bet on the EV and battery storage story.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: GXAI dipped 0.89% today to $15.57. A modest pullback on a day when the broader ASX AI-linked names were mixed. The ETF remains down around 17.5% from your entry price — though the AI sector tailwinds are real, it's been a bumpy ride so far.

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE edged down a tiny 0.21% today to $92.86. Emerging markets are being buffeted by a strong US dollar and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty (Iran, Middle East tensions). Small daily noise — nothing structural has changed.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG ticked up 0.46% today to $76.35, a quiet steady session. The diversified nature of this ETF means it captures a bit of everything — the ASX's modest gain today helped nudge it forward.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS rose 0.52% today to $526.39, reflecting the strong close on US markets last session. The big tech earnings from Google and Microsoft lifted the broader US market, and VTS tracks that whole US market, so you benefited.

watch_today.title: GOOG — Monster earnings night, long-term thesis stronger than ever
watch_today.detail: Google surged 6.88% last session after blowout Q4 earnings. AI-driven cloud revenue came in well above expectations. Your position is now up 16% overall. Nothing to do here — this is exactly what long-term holding looks like. Sit tight and let it run.

watch_today.title: MSFT — Strong Q4 earnings, Azure cloud soaring
watch_today.detail: Microsoft jumped 3.02% last session on the back of its Q4 results. Cloud revenue (Azure) surged and the market loved it. Your position is up ~4.9% overall. For a long-term holder, this is a solid compounder doing its job — no reason to change anything.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX — Still hurting, but long-term EV story intact
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals fell another 1.69% today and is down nearly 40% from your entry price. That stings. But the lithium market is cyclical — prices are low now as global EV demand growth normalises, but the structural story (batteries, EVs, energy storage) hasn't changed. Unless you think the thesis is broken, this is a hold, not a panic sell.

watch_today.title: TTWO — GTA 6 gameplay footage reportedly dropping this month
watch_today.detail: Take-Two slipped 1.82% last session, but a key catalyst is coming: GTA 6 gameplay footage is reportedly due this month. That could be a big moment for the stock. Your position is up ~4.6% overall. Worth watching closely this month — if the gameplay reveal lands well, there could be a meaningful price pop.

watch_today.title: Oil crashes 5.8% — watch for flow-on effects
watch_today.detail: Crude oil (WTI) dropped a massive 5.82% last session to $79.74 USD, likely tied to easing Iran war fears as Trump pauses strikes and peace talks restart. Cheap oil is broadly good for the economy (lower transport and energy costs) but can weigh on energy-heavy indexes. Keep an eye on how this plays out through the week.

watch_today.title: Iran tensions easing — but not over
watch_today.detail: Trump paused US strikes on Iran and announced peace talks restart today — that's why oil dropped sharply. But the situation remains fragile. The US State Department is still warning citizens to be ready to leave the Middle East. Any escalation could spike oil and rattle markets. Worth watching daily.

world.summary: The dominant global story is the US-Iran confrontation — Trump has paused strikes and peace talks are back on, but the region remains on a knife's edge. Meanwhile China is courting Europe, and oil has tanked on the de-escalation news.

stories.title: Trump pauses Iran strikes, peace talks to restart Monday
stories.why_it_matters: President Trump announced a pause in US military strikes against Iran and said peace negotiations would restart. This is a significant de-escalation after weeks of rising tensions — and the immediate market reaction was a near-6% crash in oil prices as traders priced out the risk of a wider conflict disrupting Middle Eastern oil supply. For everyday Australians, cheaper oil could eventually mean lower fuel prices, though these things take time to flow through at the pump.

stories.title: US State Department warns citizens: be ready to leave the Middle East
stories.why_it_matters: Even as Trump announced a pause in strikes, the US State Department issued a warning for American citizens in the Middle East to be prepared to leave at short notice. This signals that behind the scenes, the US government sees the situation as still very fragile. It's a reminder that the Iran crisis hasn't been resolved — just paused — and things could escalate again quickly.

stories.title: Trump's Iran 'deal' promises — eight backflips and counting
stories.why_it_matters: The SMH points out that Trump has promised an Iran 'deal' multiple times — and changed his position at least eight times. Analysts are sceptical that this latest pause in strikes will lead to a lasting agreement, given the track record. The pattern of flip-flopping means markets may be quick to re-price risk if talks break down again. Worth treating the peace-deal optimism with some healthy scepticism.

stories.title: China's Wang Yi tours Nordic Europe, pitching warmer ties
stories.why_it_matters: China's top diplomat Wang Yi is touring Scandinavia and Nordic Europe, pushing to reset and deepen China-Europe relations. This matters because it reflects China's effort to drive a wedge between the US and its European allies at a time of intense US-China tension. For Australia, closer China-Europe ties could reshape global trade dynamics and affect demand for Australian exports like iron ore and energy.

stories.title: The collapse of national sovereignty in the Middle East
stories.why_it_matters: A broader analysis piece from Responsible Statecraft argues that the ongoing conflicts across the Middle East — from Gaza to Lebanon to Iran — represent a deeper erosion of stable national borders and government authority in the region. The argument is that US and regional interventions have weakened state structures rather than strengthened them. For global investors, this kind of long-term regional instability is a persistent risk premium baked into oil prices and defence spending.

markets.summary: Last night's US session was a cracker — Google and Microsoft earnings drove the NASDAQ up 1% and the S&P 500 up 0.7%. The ASX closed today up 0.47%. The big shock was oil crashing nearly 6% as Iran tensions eased. Gold hit a new high of $4,115 USD as investors keep one foot in safe havens.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Solid session today, lifted by big tech tailwinds from Wall Street overnight and broad market strength.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Strong close last night driven by Google and Microsoft earnings beats. The index is at elevated levels.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Tech-heavy NASDAQ jumped 1% last session as Google surged 6.9% and Microsoft added 3% post-earnings.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil crashed nearly 6% as Trump paused Iran strikes and peace talks restarted — a huge single-session move.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold hit another record high, now above $4,100 USD. Investors are keeping safe-haven exposure despite the Iran de-escalation.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar was essentially flat, holding just above 70 US cents.

politics.summary: The main domestic story today is a new RBA survey revealing a fundamental misunderstanding most Australians have about how interest rates and inflation interact — with big implications for public trust in the Reserve Bank.

stories.title: Most Australians think rate rises cause inflation — RBA survey
stories.why_it_matters: A new Reserve Bank of Australia survey has found that most Australians believe interest rate rises actually cause inflation to go up — the opposite of how it works. In reality, the RBA raises rates to slow spending and bring inflation down. This widespread misunderstanding matters because it means many Australians are angry at the RBA for something they think it's doing wrong — when in fact it's doing its job. It also makes the RBA's communication job harder: if the public doesn't understand the mechanism, they're more likely to distrust the bank's decisions and demand political interference.

ai.summary: The big AI story today is regulatory: the EU's AI Act rules are now officially enforceable, making August 2, 2026 a landmark date for AI governance worldwide. Meanwhile, a debate is heating up about whether the US Congress will follow Europe's lead.

stories.title: EU AI Act rules become enforceable — what changes now?
stories.why_it_matters: As of August 2, 2026, the European Union's AI Act — the world's first comprehensive legal framework for artificial intelligence — is now fully enforceable. This means AI companies operating in Europe must comply with rules around transparency, safety testing, and bans on certain high-risk uses (like real-time facial recognition in public). Companies that don't comply face fines of up to €35 million or 7% of global revenue. This affects any company selling AI products in Europe — including Google, Microsoft, and others — and sets a global benchmark that other countries, including Australia, are watching closely.

stories.title: Business leaders are now legally accountable for AI — August 2 milestone
stories.why_it_matters: Alongside the EU AI Act coming into force, today marks a broader shift: corporate executives are now personally and legally accountable for the AI systems their companies deploy. This is a significant change from the 'move fast and break things' era — CEOs and boards can no longer claim ignorance if an AI system causes harm or discriminates. For investors, this means AI risk is now a boardroom governance issue, not just a tech team problem, which could slow some AI deployments but also reduce long-term liability risks.

stories.title: Most Americans want AI regulation — will Congress act?
stories.why_it_matters: A USA Today opinion piece highlights polling showing most Americans support some form of AI regulation — but Congress has so far failed to pass any meaningful federal AI law. With the EU now enforcing its rules, there's growing pressure on Washington to catch up. For investors in AI-exposed stocks like Google and Microsoft, US regulation is a slow-moving but real risk to watch: too heavy-handed and it could crimp growth, but well-designed rules could actually provide more market certainty.

stories.title: One dashboard, 20+ AI models for $79 — the AI toolbox gets cheaper
stories.why_it_matters: A new AI subscription service is offering access to more than 20 AI models — including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and others — through a single dashboard for $79. This kind of product shows how rapidly AI tools are being commoditised and bundled. For everyday users, it means powerful AI is getting cheaper and easier to access. For investors, it raises a question: if AI access becomes a commodity, do the big model makers (Google, Microsoft/OpenAI, Anthropic) maintain their pricing power long-term?

sport.summary: NRL Round 22 is done and dusted with some big talking points heading into Round 23. In the AFL, Adelaide cruised into the top four. Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova is eyeing the US Open, and Aryna Sabalenka goes in as a firm favourite.

stories.title: Bellamy's brutal warning and Panthers hit with big blow — Round 23 team tips
stories.why_it_matters: Storm coach Craig Bellamy has issued a blunt warning that at least one player 'won't be playing' in Round 23, suggesting a selection axing rather than injury. The Panthers are also dealing with a significant injury blow heading into their clash against the Warriors at Go Media Stadium on Friday night — bad timing given how tight the top-four race is. The Titans host the Cowboys on Thursday night at Cbus Super Stadium — a home game on the Gold Coast worth keeping an eye on.

stories.title: Eels beat Tigers, Hynes chases NRL points record — Round 22 wrap
stories.why_it_matters: Parramatta Eels beat Wests Tigers in Round 22, with the win partly aided by 'rubbish' play from South Sydney Rabbitohs (who the Eels also faced in this report). Penrith's Dylan Edwards or Roosters' James Tedesco rival, Roosters playmaker Sam Walker or Dolphins halfback — actually it's Dolphins halfback Isaiya Katoa who is reportedly chasing an NRL points-scoring record. Key result for the finals picture as teams jockey for position with the finals just weeks away.

stories.title: Sharks forward hit with $6,600 in fines after 'ridiculous' sin bin
stories.why_it_matters: A Cronulla Sharks forward was slapped with $6,600 in fines after a sin bin that the NRL Match Review Committee called 'ridiculous.' The incident adds scrutiny to the NRL's sin bin process and whether the punishment fits the crime — a debate that keeps flaring up in the game. The Sharks face the Dragons on Sunday in Round 23.

stories.title: Adelaide Crows cruise past Essendon Bombers, move into AFL top four
stories.why_it_matters: Adelaide Crows cruised to a convincing win over Essendon Bombers on the weekend, moving into the top four of the AFL ladder. It's a significant result for a Crows side that looked shaky earlier in the season — they're now genuine finals contenders. Meanwhile, Melbourne Demons ground out a win on the Gold Coast, and Richmond Tigers climbed off the bottom of the ladder.

stories.title: Wimbledon champion Noskova eyes 'new opportunity' at US Open
stories.why_it_matters: Czech player Linda Noskova, fresh off her Wimbledon title, says she's approaching the US Open as a 'new opportunity' rather than feeling pressure to back up. Meanwhile, world number one Aryna Sabalenka is heading into the US Open warmup events with high confidence after a strong hard-court season. The US Open hardcourt swing is underway — the big names are in form and the draw is shaping up to be a cracker.
